name: Pairing sequences with language
gist: Bridging time series and text by learning from paired descriptions, using language models to reason about sequences, or generating narratives from temporal data.
explain: Numbers tell part of the story, but context is in text. A hospital chart has vital signs and also doctor's notes describing what is happening: 'patient admitted with fever, responding to antibiotics.' A factory has sensor logs and also maintenance records: 'bearing installed 200 hours ago, last lubricated Thursday.' Stock data has prices and also news headlines and earnings call transcripts. Language carries information that is hard to encode as numbers because context and causation are described in words, not as numerical features. Language models have become skilled at reasoning and synthesis, so a natural question is: can we use language to help time series models, since language encodes domain knowledge that numbers alone do not capture?

The connection is surprisingly deep. First, language can provide supervision. If a doctor annotates a time series—'this pattern signals sepsis'—that labeled data is precious for training. Second, language can augment learning. A model that sees both the time series and paired descriptions might learn more stable patterns because descriptions highlight what humans think matters. Third, language models themselves can reason about sequences. Given a price chart and news, a language model might generate a narrative: 'stock fell because earnings missed estimates.' This is reasoning, not just pattern matching. Fourth, language can be the output: instead of predicting the next price, predict a description like 'stock will be stable.' This bridges two modalities.

Papers in this cluster train multimodal models that jointly encode time series and text. Some use pretraining: learn general patterns from large unlabeled time series, then adapt to new sequences with small amounts of paired text and data. Others use language as a regularizer: if the model's internal state is interpretable and can be described in language, that forces the model to be more human-aligned. A few papers generate narratives from sequences—they produce coherent descriptions of what the sequence is doing. The underlying insight is that language forces structure and interpretability in a way that raw sequence modeling often lacks.

papers.title: Language in the Flow of Time: Time-Series-Paired Texts Weaved into a Unified Temporal Narrative
papers.contribution: TaTS enhances multimodal predictive performance on forecasting and imputation tasks without modifying model architectures across various benchmark datasets.

papers.title: Long-range Modeling and Processing of Multimodal Event Sequences
papers.contribution: Outperforms baselines on predictive accuracy and quality of generated textual analyses, including on the DanmakuTPP-QA benchmark.

papers.title: Semantic-Enhanced Time-Series Forecasting via Large Language Models
papers.contribution: Achieves superior forecasting performance while reducing computational cost by freezing the LLM and reducing sequence dimensionality.

papers.title: Sonar-TS: Search-Then-Verify Natural Language Querying for Time Series Databases
papers.contribution: Introduces NLQTSBench, the first large-scale benchmark for NLQ over TSDB-scale histories, demonstrating Sonar-TS effectively navigates complex temporal queries.

papers.title: Unlocking the Value of Text: Event-Driven Reasoning and Multi-Level Alignment for Time Series Forecasting
papers.contribution: Demonstrates significant improvements on real-world datasets across 10 domains, validating effectiveness of unlocking text value for time series forecasting.

papers.title: Can we generate portable representations for clinical time series data using LLMs?
papers.contribution: Achieves competitive performance in-distribution while exhibiting smaller relative performance drops when transferring to new hospitals across MIMIC-IV, HIRID, and PPICU datasets.

papers.title: From Text to Forecasts: Bridging Modality Gap with Temporal Evolution Semantic Space
papers.contribution: TESS achieves up to 29% reduction in forecasting error compared to unimodal and multimodal baselines by bridging modality gap via semantic primitives.

papers.title: Multi-Scale Hypergraph Meets LLMs: Aligning Large Language Models for Time Series Analysis
papers.contribution: MSH-LLM achieves state-of-the-art results on 27 datasets across 5 applications by leveraging multi-scale alignment.

papers.title: Overcoming the Modality Gap in Context-Aided Forecasting
papers.contribution: Demonstrates context utilization and substantial improvements in context-aided forecasting by showing that dataset quality is a major bottleneck and verified context improves model training.

papers.title: Rethinking Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting Evaluation
papers.contribution: Simple ensemble methods leveraging rich textual context outperform strong baselines; reveals many approaches that perform well on existing benchmarks fail on TimesX.

papers.title: Time Series Reasoning via Process-Verifiable Thinking Data Synthesis and Scheduling for Tailored LLM Reasoning
papers.contribution: Notably, it enables compact 3B–4B models to achieve reasoning capabilities on par with or exceeding those of larger proprietary LLMs

papers.title: TimeOmni-1: Incentivizing Complex Reasoning with Time Series in Large Language Models
papers.contribution: First unified time series reasoning model designed to address diverse real-world problems demanding time series reasoning with multi-stage training.

papers.title: TsLLM: Augmenting LLMs for General Time Series Understanding and Prediction
papers.contribution: TsLLM integrates time series analysis with natural language reasoning on tasks requiring both; demonstrates strong zero-shot and few-shot performance.
